title: U.S. stock futures steady after Nasdaq posts worst day since June
full_text:
Nasdaq posts worst day since June as AI financing worries batter risk sentiment
Investing.com-- U.S. stock futures were little changed on Thursday evening after Wall Street ended sharply lower, with the Nasdaq Composite posting its steepest daily decline since June amid concerns over the cost and financing of artificial intelligence investments.
S&P 500 Futures traded largely flat at 7,707.0 points, while Nasdaq 100 Futures fell 0.2% to 29,083.75 points by 20:10 ET (00:10 GMT). Dow Jones Futures edged up 0.1% to 53,133.0 points.

In the regular session, the NASDAQ Composite fell 2.6% to 26,008.86, while the S&P 500 lost 1.2% to 7,663.43. The Dow Jones Industrial Average ended flat at 52,867.98, as investors shifted away from growth-oriented technology stocks toward more defensive sectors.
The selloff reflected growing scrutiny of the massive capital spending required to develop AI infrastructure, even as companies report strong demand for computing capacity and AI-related services.
Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) shares tumbled nearly 7% after the Facebook parent reported its first cash outflow in more than a decade, driven by AI-related expenditure, and announced plans to issue non-voting shares to help finance its growth.
Although quarterly revenue beat analysts' expectations, the company's spending plans heightened concerns about the returns on its investments.
Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) shares fell about 3.1% after the electric-vehicle maker cut its 2026 capital expenditure forecast, adding to uncertainty over the pace of its AI and robotics expansion.
Semiconductor stocks were hit particularly hard, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropping 6.7%, its biggest daily decline since June 23.
The selloff also hit AI-related infrastructure companies, including CoreWeave Inc (NASDAQ:CRWV), highlighting concerns over financing costs and the time required to generate returns from heavy investment.
Oil prices added to the uncertain outlook. Brent crude settled up 4% at $113.17 a barrel, its highest since May 4. Fresh Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia fuelled concerns about disruptions to Middle Eastern energy supplies, raising the prospect of renewed inflationary pressure.
Investors sought safety in government bonds, sending the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield down nearly 20 basis points to around 4.95%, its biggest daily decline since March 2023. The move reflected a shift toward safer assets amid concerns about technology valuations and geopolitical risks.
Despite the technology rout, corporate earnings offered some support. Procter & Gamble (NYSE:PG) rose after reporting better-than-expected quarterly results, while Spotify (NYSE:SPOT) gained on a stronger operating income outlook.
Investors will now look for further earnings updates and fresh economic data to gauge whether the technology selloff signals a broader reassessment of growth prospects or a temporary correction in AI-related shares.
The Federal Reserve's policy decision next week will also be in focus, particularly as higher energy prices threaten to complicate the inflation outlook.

title: Japan CPI inflation hits 9-mth high in Sept, crosses BOJ target
full_text:
Nasdaq posts worst day since June as AI financing worries batter risk sentiment
Investing.com-- Japanese consumer inflation rose as expected in September, with core inflation hitting a nine-month high and crossing the Bank of Japan’s annual target amid continued pressure from rising energy costs and a soft yen.
Core consumer price index inflation, which excludes volatile fresh food prices, rose 2.1% year-on-year in September, data from the Statistics Bureau showed on Friday.
The print was the strongest reading since December 2025, was in line with expectations, and accelerated from the 1.7% rise seen in the prior month.
A core reading that excludes both fresh food and energy prices jumped to a 10-month high of 2.5% from 2.0% in September. The print is closely watched by the BOJ as a gauge of underlying inflation.
Headline CPI rose 2.1% year-on-year from 1.9% in the prior month.
Get more insights on Japan and the BOJ by subscribing to InvestingPro-- with up to 50% off
Inflation was largely broad-based, as rising business costs– due to high energy prices and other global supply chain disruptions– trickled down into consumer prices. Japanese producer inflation hit a 3-½ year high earlier this year.
A soft yen also factored into higher inflation, especially as Japan’s import costs increased.
While government subsidies on consumer fuel costs blunted the direct impact of soaring global oil prices, they are expected to still underpin Japanese inflation, especially as businesses pass on higher costs to consumers.
Oil prices hit a five-month high this week on worsening geopolitical conditions in the Middle East. Japan is a major importer of oil and gas, and was especially hit by soaring crude costs.
Friday’s data showed core inflation rising past the BOJ’s 2% annual target– a trend that is likely to give the central bank more impetus to keep raising interest rates.
"With underlying inflation back above the Bank of Japan’s 2% target, the case for further tightening remains on solid ground," Capital Economics analysts said in a note.
"With Governor (Kazuo) Ueda recently warning that underlying inflation is already close to the BoJ’s 2% target and that “we cannot tolerate it rising any further”, we think the Bank is firmly on track to raise rates further," they said.
The central bank raised rates by a cumulative 50 basis points this year, and has signaled plans for more hikes, especially if inflation continues to tick higher.
Friday’s print also furthered expectations that the BOJ will discuss more rate hikes when it meets next week. Recent media reports said the BOJ is preparing to hike its inflation forecasts at its October meeting.

title: Japan considers ending gasoline subsidies in December- Reuters
full_text:
Investing.com -- Japan’s government is considering reducing gasoline subsidies starting in December due to concerns about depleting funds, Reuters reported on Friday, citing two ruling party officials.
The government and ruling coalition are discussing a proposal to gradually reduce weekly subsidies paid to fuel distributors. Under this plan, average retail gasoline prices would increase to around 175 yen per liter in December and 180 yen in January, the Reuters report said.
Tokyo had doled out the emergency subsidies in March to protect households and businesses from rising oil prices after the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran started.
The program costs the government several billion dollars each month to maintain the nationwide average price of regular gasoline at approximately 170 yen ($1.09) per liter. This spending is quickly using up the 3.1 trillion yen supplementary budget that was approved in June, as crude oil prices remain high.
An end to the subsidies risks a sharp increase in Japanese consumer inflation, which has so far remained relatively muted despite soaring oil and gas prices. Japanese producer inflation, however, rose sharply this year on growing fuel costs.

title: Japan factory activity slows in Oct, services improve, PMI shows
full_text:
Investing.com-- Japanese manufacturing activity expanded at a slower pace in October while services sector growth strengthened, a private-sector survey showed on Friday, as rising input costs and weakening demand weighed on the outlook.
The S&P Global flash manufacturing PMI fell to 53.3 in October from 54.1 in September, missing estimates of 54.5. It remained above the 50 mark that separates growth from contraction.
The services PMI rose to 52.0 from 51.3, while the flash composite PMI, which covers both sectors, held steady at 52.3, indicating private-sector activity expanded for a 19th consecutive month.
Manufacturing output growth slowed to its weakest pace in seven months, while overall new order growth eased to a three-month low. Export orders continued to increase, but at the slowest rate in four months.
Input cost inflation accelerated slightly, driven by higher raw material and labour costs, and higher energy prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict.
Business confidence also weakened, with inflation concerns weighing on expectations for the year ahead, the survey showed.

title: Japan government, BOJ gap on inflation laid bare ahead of key policy meeting
full_text:
Nasdaq posts worst day since June as AI financing worries batter risk sentiment
By Leika Kihara
TOKYO, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Japan has yet to meet the conditions for officially declaring victory over deflation, Economy Minister Minoru Kiuchi said on Friday, exposing a divide with the Bank of Japan as it sees the economy on the cusp of durably achieving its 2% inflation goal.
Kiuchi’s remarks, from a close ally of dovish Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, underscore a disconnect between the government and the BOJ on price moves.
They also come ahead of the BOJ’s policy meeting next week, when it is seen signalling that underlying inflation has hit its 2% target as the Iran war-induced energy shock and rising import costs from a weak yen push up prices.
The government, however, has stopped short of declaring victory over deflation, saying it needs clearer evidence that the economy will not slide back into a period of persistent price declines.
"We need to be cautious in making the decision and look comprehensively at consumer price moves, GDP deflator and factors driving underlying inflation," Kiuchi said when asked whether the government could formally declare an end to deflation.
"It’s important that Japan does not revert to deflation," he said, adding it was premature to declare an end to deflation.
Kiuchi made the remarks at a news conference, when asked how the government will align its view on deflation with the BOJ’s assessment that underlying inflation may have hit its target.
While fuel subsidies have helped temper price pressures, core consumer inflation has hovered near the BOJ’s 2% target for four years, challenging the government’s view that Japan has yet to fully escape deflation.
The core consumer price index (CPI), which excludes volatile fresh food but includes fuel costs, rose 2.1% in September from a year earlier, data showed on Friday.
Some analysts say the government’s reluctance to declare an end to deflation reflects concern that doing so would narrow its room to pursue accommodative fiscal and monetary policy.
Declaring an official end to deflation could also draw calls to tweak a joint government-BOJ statement, signed in 2013, pledging coordinated efforts by the two sides to end deflation including by "pursuing monetary easing to achieve the BOJ’s inflation target at the earliest date possible." The government and BOJ reaffirmed the joint statement in 2025.
"I hope the BOJ conducts monetary policy appropriately to stably and sustainably achieve its 2% inflation target, taking into account the principles of the joint BOJ-government statement," Kiuchi said.
Considered an advocate of loose monetary policy, Kiuchi has repeatedly signaled his reservation over the BOJ’s rate-hike plans.
Kiuchi said on Tuesday he hoped to attend the central bank’s policy meeting next week, when it is seen keeping interest rates steady, but revising up its inflation forecast and signalling its resolve to keep hiking borrowing costs.

title: European shares slip as French fiscal turmoil drives weekly loss

title: UK retail sales fall as consumer confidence tumbles
full_text:
By William Schomberg
LONDON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - British consumers reined in their shopping in September as a warm start to the autumn hurt clothing sales and higher fuel prices ate into household budgets, while separate data showed confidence levels plunged in October.
Retail sales volumes dropped by 0.4% in September from August, a bigger decline than a fall of 0.1% expected by most economists in a Reuters poll.
British shoppers had surprised analysts with the strength of their spending in recent months, even as the conflict in the Gulf pushes up fuel and domestic energy prices.
Britain’s two biggest food retailers Tesco and Sainsbury’s, fast-food chain Greggs and home improvement retailer Kingfisher all recently upgraded their annual profit guidance.
Over the three months to September, total sales volumes rose by 0.7%, helped by the soccer World Cup and a summer heatwave, according to the Office for National Statistics which revised up its monthly figures for August and July.
However, major retailers have highlighted the challenging conditions for consumers ahead of next week’s budget announcement by finance minister John Healey - who has promised a bit more help with the cost of living - and signs of more inflation pressure in 2027.
Supermarket sales fell in September after growth in July and August, the ONS said.
A survey published earlier on Friday showed consumer confidence in October suffered its sharpest month-on-month fall since early in the COVID-19 pandemic. Excluding the pandemic, the last similar-sized drop followed the June 2016 Brexit vote.
“The drop in retail sales in September and sharp fall in consumer confidence in October raises the risk that the economy’s recent run of resilience might be coming to an end," Thomas Pugh, chief economist at accountancy firm RSM UK, said.
Analysts at consultancy Pantheon Macroeconomics said it was unclear if the drop was due to worries about the budget, a fading of the boost to confidence seen after Andy Burnham became prime minister or something more fundamental.
"Confidence had been at a two-year high. But it seems likely that overall GDP growth will ease sharply from the 0.7% quarter-to-quarter pace it is on track for in Q3. We look for quarterly growth of 0.2% in Q4," they said.
The ONS said fuel sales volumes in September rose by 2.2% from August when drivers filled up their tanks only partially in response to the jump in fuel prices caused by the Iran war.
The value of spending on fuel rose by more than 6% in September following a similar month-on-month increase in August.
That pressure on household spending is unlikely to abate quickly - Brent crude oil prices hit a five-month peak of $114.10 a barrel on Friday on fears of an escalation of the conflict in the Middle East.

title: Take Five: AI trade meets the Fed
full_text:
Oct 23 (Reuters) - An eye-catching week is in store as rate-setters at the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan announce policy decisions, while investors will gauge whether results from Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft can fuel the next leg of the AI rally.
An election in Brazil, a gathering of China’s top leadership and a closely watched British budget add political risk to the agenda.
Here’s all you need to know about the coming week in financial markets by Lewis Krauskopf in New York, Kevin Buckland in Tokyo, and Dhara Ranasinghe, Marc Jones and William Schomberg in London.
1/ MOVE OVER
It’s a packed week for central banks. The Fed, Bank of Canada and Reserve Bank of New Zealand meet on Wednesday, the ECB on Thursday, and the BOJ a day later.
The Fed, ECB and BOJ face no immediate pressure to hike rates after tightening last month.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will be pressed on his view on the rate outlook. The ECB is sure to face questions about surging French borrowing costs that risk becoming a flashpoint, while the BOJ may raise its inflation forecasts in a post-meeting report.
Markets expect Canada and New Zealand to hike rates to contain inflation, with all policymakers grappling with the extent to which high oil will fuel broader price pressures.
2/ HYPERSCALER HOT SEAT
A big week for US corporate earnings will be headlined by reports from three of the largest companies at the heart of the huge AI capital investment theme that has driven up equities.
Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon — three of the so-called hyperscalers — will post results at a time investors are becoming wary of the risks of the spending on data centres.
The week will be critical to determining if the third quarter lived up to high expectations for US profit growth, with about one-third of S&P 500 companies reporting.
Other high-profile firms set to report include drugmaker Eli Lilly, oil majors Exxon and Chevron, and industrial equipment giant Caterpillar.
3/ FISCAL TIGHTROPE
British finance minister John Healey will announce his first budget on Wednesday, when he will try to offer some relief from higher energy prices to households, but without unsettling the bond market by ramping up borrowing.
That means Healey may have to accept a narrowing of his room for manoeuvre to meet his fiscal rules. Analysts polled by Reuters think he can allow his headroom to almost halve to around £15 billion ($20 billion) without spooking the market.
Banks might bear the brunt of tax increases, and the share prices of Britain’s biggest lenders have fallen in the run-up to Healey’s high-profile debut.
Bigger decisions on spending in areas such as defence, public services and welfare are likely to be put off until next year, with Healey hoping the Iran war — and the pressure it is putting on government borrowing costs — may have abated by then.
4/ NETANYAHU’S MOMENT OF TRUTH
Israel’s election on Tuesday is poised to be one of the most consequential in the country’s history.
Polls have it as a coin toss, with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud bloc nor an opposition centred around former military chief Gadi Eisenkot expected to win a majority, raising the prospect of lengthy coalition negotiations.
Yet for markets, it also comes after an extraordinary rally in Israeli assets. Since 2023’s October 7 attacks, the Tel Aviv stock market has surged more than 135%, while the shekel is up a world-beating 25%.
Analysts are quick to point out the AI boom has been key, given Israel’s tech expertise, and will remain so. But investors also see the potential for tensions to be gradually dialled down in the longer term if Eisenkot and his allies can win out.
5/ PARTY PRIORITIES
China’s top leadership gathers in Beijing for the four-day Fifth Plenum from Monday, with officials deliberating on "Advancing Full and Rigorous Party Self-Governance."
That may sound inward-looking, but official Chinese commentary frames the initiative as an effort to strengthen Party discipline and execution in response to a more challenging external environment, including an increasingly tense relationship with the United States and curbs on China’s access to advanced foreign technology.
That’s not to say Beijing doesn’t face challenges at home too, with domestic demand stuck in a prolonged slump that has proved stubbornly resistant to stimulus efforts.

title: Volvo Cars sinks 27% as it swings to Q3 loss, plans 2,500 job cuts
full_text:
Investing.com -- Volvo Cars (ST:VOLCARb) shares sank more than 28% in early Stockholm trading Friday after the company swung to a third-quarter operating loss of 3.7 billion Swedish crowns and said it would cut about 2,500 jobs, as price wars in China and U.S. tariffs hit sales at the Geely-owned carmaker.
That figure excludes joint ventures and associates and items affecting comparability.
A year earlier, the profit on the same basis was SEK 5.8 billion, with a margin of 6.7%; this quarter’s margin was -5.6%.
Including those items, operating income was a loss of SEK 5.6 billion versus a profit of SEK 6.4 billion a year earlier, and the margin was -8.4% versus 7.4% a year earlier. Revenue was SEK 66.9 billion versus SEK 86.4 billion a year earlier, and 10% below the consensus estimates.
Jefferies analysts attributed the revenue miss to weak wholesale volumes. "Wholesales -19% y/y are the main surprise with a sizeable destocking, FX was incrementally worse and Other (parts, used cars, lithium hedge, tariffs, emission credits) -2.8bn y/y," they wrote.
In China, revenue fell by almost 50% year-on-year as Volvo Cars and other legacy premium brands faced fierce competition from new Chinese rivals and severe pricing pressure.
In the United States, tariffs and the removal of consumer incentives for electrified cars continued to squeeze margins.
The quarter also took a SEK 1.1 billion hit from a negative revaluation of CAFE credits because of legislation changes in the United States, along with negative raw material developments and a SEK 0.9 billion negative effect from recognising Polestar’s losses in the second quarter of 2026.
Basic loss per share was SEK 1.63 versus earnings of SEK 1.75 a year earlier. Free cash flow was negative SEK 8.9 billion versus negative SEK 4.3 billion a year earlier, with China and the United States weighing on cash flow.
Volvo Cars aims to cut a further SEK 5 billion in indirect spending and variable costs, on top of earlier cost programmes, and will reduce about 2,500 jobs globally, 2,000 of them in Sweden, by ending consultant contracts, through natural attrition and with targeted exit packages.
The full effect will come by the end of 2027, when indirect spending will be almost 25% lower than in 2024.
It will focus on five dedicated Volvo plants and is exploring multi-brand assembly with Geely at its Chengdu and Ghent plants.
Fully electric cars made up 32% of sales versus 22% a year earlier, and 45% in Europe. The EX60 has over 50,000 European orders, but production is ramping up more slowly than planned.
"However, in the short term, with severely challenged volumes, we need to reinforce our turnaround plan with additional decisive actions," CEO Håkan Samuelsson said.
Vahid Karaahmetovic contributed to this report.
